name: CCW Heavyweight Championship
aka: CCW Heavyweight Championship of the World
notes: The alliance's own member profile of the fed calls it the World Heavyweight Championship in its champions block and the CCW Heavyweight Title in its own history on the same page; the fed's own ring announcer reads it out at Revolution as the CCW Heavyweight Championship of the World. Every form is the record's own.
epitaph: Nineteen men are named as having held it, and the fed named them itself: Revolution opens on a montage of nineteen former champions flickering past with the belt, from The Supreme Machine through Ghettodogg, Hardcore Gorilla Mask and El Mierda to Jason McAllister. Almost none of those reigns is recoverable. What the record does hold is the shape of the belt's own crises — a 104-day reign by Phil Burner in 2000 that the fed still called its record, a month in the spring of 2002 when its own rankings listed the title vacant and two men tied at the top, Blayze losing it at Revolution after pulling the referee into a charge, and Legacy taking it off Jason Dread in January 2005 and putting him through a table on his way out of the ring. That is where the record stops.

name: CCW Hardcore Championship
notes: Named in the fed's own 2004 rulebook among five championships, two years after the alliance's profile page and one year after the only change of it the record holds.
epitaph: It was fought for with barbed wire. The one title change held is Revolution's opener, where Enigma beat Jack Manson in a match whose props were a trash can wrapped in barbed wire and a board of nails pulled out of a bin bag, and the belt changed hands on a referee's decision Manson spent the rest of the night calling a screw job. Scorpion held it in the spring of 2002 and Brad Douglas was billed the champion in the first week of March 2003; nothing held says how it travelled between any of them.

name: CCW Independent Championship
notes: The fed's own magazine calls it the Independant Title in its own card listing; the ring announcer reads it as the CCW Independent Championship.
epitaph: A belt defended at Revolution with the champion and the challenger tied together at the wrist. The ring announcer read the rules out before the bell — pinfall, submission, or touching all four corners in turn — and Scorpion kept it against Dan Logan, having already been billed the holder of it that same month. Kensuke Suzahara was the champion a year earlier and fourth on the fed's own top ten the week that list was written.

name: CCW Women's Championship
epitaph: The federation ran a women's division from 1999 and kept running one to the end of what survives; three women's matches opened the Lockdown before Revolution and two more were on the card the last time it advertised one. Devyl's own card claims four reigns with it and an award for the longest of them. The one change held is Revolution's, where Sheena Ramone took it from Lacey Skye Morris by disqualification — a decision the fed declared and the record keeps as declared.

name: CCW Trans-Atlantic Championship
notes: Two years later the fed's own rulebook lists an Atlantic Championship instead, among five belts, with no Trans-Atlantic Championship beside it and no explanation of a rename. That belt is recorded separately, as ccw-atlantic; nothing held joins the two lineages.
epitaph: The second belt on the card, and the one whose own name did not survive the fed's last era intact. Michael "Spitfire" Stevens won it out of a three-way against Gobstopper and Ace Hawk at Revolution; a year earlier the alliance's own profile page named The Valiant One the champion in its champions block and Brad Lamen the champion in its own top ten, on the same page, in the same month. Both readings are kept.

name: CCW Atlantic Championship
notes: Named only in the fed's own rulebook of 7 December 2004, second in a list of five championships. Whether it is the Trans-Atlantic Championship of 2003 under a shortened name or a belt of its own is not something the record answers.
epitaph: A line in a rulebook. The federation's own championships page for it was captured as an empty template, and no champion of it is named anywhere in the surviving record.

name: CCW International Championship
notes: Named only in the fed's own rulebook of 7 December 2004, third in a list of five championships.
epitaph: The federation listed it third among its own five belts in December 2004 and built a page for it. The page was captured blank, the rulebook line is the whole of the evidence, and no holder of it survives.

name: CCW Tag Team Championship
epitaph: It was vacant in the spring of 2003 and the fed filled it with a tournament: a Tag Team Lethal Lottery drawn by the president, a four-team elimination match that ran forty-three minutes and sent one team forward, and a three-team ladder match at Revolution that Adam Christ and Jack Manson won by pinning Damien Nhyte. Neither man waited to be announced; they took the belts and left through the crowd. A year earlier the Blood Brothers held them, and one of the Blood Brothers was billed the world champion on the same page.

name: CCW Pacific Championship
notes: Attested once, in the alliance's own member profile of the fed. It is absent from the fed's own 2004 rulebook list and from every 2003 document held.
epitaph: John Jupiter held it in the spring of 2002 and stood third on the federation's own list of its ten best that March. One page names the belt, once; by the time the fed wrote its rules down again it was listing five championships and this was not one of them.

name: CCW Lightweight Championship
epitaph: Billed as held by El Mierda heading into a December 1999 defense; no surviving document confirms the outcome.
